title: Toronto cop charged with manslaughter in teen Chadd Facey's death after 'Kijiji deal gone bad'
subtitle: Eight-year veteran Const. Calvin Au has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated assault. The Star has previously reported Facey died in hospital after a dispute with Au and another off-duty officer.
article: Nearly two years after the sudden death of a Black teen in Brampton, a Toronto police officer has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated assault - a "shocking" development and an exceedingly rare case of an off-duty cop charged in a homicide.

Ontario's police watchdog announced Friday that Const. Calvin Au, a 33-year-old officer with eight years on the job, has been charged in connection to the April 26, 2021, death of Chadd Facey. A 19-year-old psychology student and aspiring hip-hop artist, Facey died just hours after an alleged "struggle" with the cop in a Brampton park.

The confrontation between Au and Facey - allegedly brought on by "Kijiji deal gone bad" - went unreported for nearly four months. The Special Investigations Unit, the watchdog that investigates police, only took over the case after Peel Regional Police investigators probing Facey's death discovered he had had a physical struggle with Au in his final hours.
All the while, Facey's mother waited to find out what happened to her son .

"It has been clear to our family that there was some kind of misconduct that had occurred in respect of Chadd's death," Fay Fagan said Friday. "We are happy to finally see that the officer is being held accountable for his actions."

As is typical in cases when the watchdog lays criminal charges against an officer, the SIU has not detailed the evidence against Au to preserve his fair trial interests. The SIU also has not released Facey's cause of death.

Au has been suspended with pay, a police spokesperson confirmed. Peter Brauti, his lawyer, said he was "obviously disappointed that the SIU laid these charges" but wouldn't comment while the case is before the courts.

As first reported by the Star in April , Au faces separate police misconduct charges stemming from Facey's death. According to the police documents filed in that case - which have not been tested at the disciplinary tribunal - the incident began when Au and his Toronto police colleague, Const. Gurmakh Benning, went to Brampton's Bellchase Trail and Highway 50 to buy an Apple watch from Facey; the SIU has said the men met up between 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m. (Benning is not criminally charged).

Then, believing the watch was fake, the officer allegedly chased Facey down by car and then by foot. According to the documents, Au took Facey to the ground and then held him down as the teen tried to get up.

According to his mother, Facey returned home around 5 p.m., obviously unwell. Medical records seen by the Star show that he didn't know his own name and had a "hematoma" - a pooling of blood - on his head prior to being rushed to Brampton Civic Hospital around 5:35 p.m. By 8:58 p.m., Facey had a seizure that eventually led to a "code blue," meaning respiratory or cardiac arrest, according to the medical documents. He died soon after.

The hospital contacted Peel Regional Police, which launched a sudden-death investigation to determine what happened in Facey's final hours. It wasn't until August 2021 - when a Peel investigator reviewed Facey's cellphone records, which linked him to Benning's phone - that the officers' involvement was discovered, according to the police tribunal documents.
Peel police contacted Toronto police, which then notified the SIU "immediately," a Toronto police spokesperson said.

The documents allege Au and Benning repeatedly failed to report their involvement for several months after the incident, starting moments after the alleged takedown when they neglected to identify themselves as police officers when Gurmakh initially dialed 911 to report the altercation.

"You had placed a call to 911 indicating that it was a 'Kijiji deal that had gone bad,' but did not identify yourself as a police officer on the call and eventually advised the call taker that the matter was resolved," according to documents outlining the allegations against Benning.

Au and Benning allegedly failed to notify Peel Regional Police about the incident and later, after Peel cops discovered their connection to Facey's final hours, neither cop told Toronto police they were involved in an "active criminal investigation," the documents allege. The pair also failed to properly handle the evidence - the Apple watch - in accordance with the Toronto police property procedure, the documents allege.
It's not known if Facey ever knew Au and Benning were off-duty police officers; Facey's mother said she was blindsided when she found out.
"When I heard that police were involved, I was just numb," Fagan said in an interview last year.

The SIU took over the investigation in August 2021. The watchdog, which probes injuries and deaths involving police, will investigate off-duty officers under certain circumstances, including when a cop uses police powers off the clock, such as launching a pursuit of someone, as is alleged in this case.
Asha James, the lawyer for Facey's family, said the charge sends "a clear message that whether on duty or off duty, police are not immune from being held accountable for their wrongful conduct."
"The facts of the case as presented are shocking," said Julius Haag, assistant professor of sociology at the University of Toronto whose research includes policing.

It is not the first time the SIU has charged a Toronto police officer in connection to an off-duty assault. In 2017, Toronto police Const. Michael Theriault was charged with offences including aggravated assault for the off-duty beating of Dafonte Miller, a Black teen who was injured so severely his eye had to be removed. Theriault was convicted of assault and sentenced to nine months in jail.
There are clear parallels with the Miller case, which also went unreported to the SIU for months, said University of Toronto criminologist Scot Wortley.

"How frequently does this take place?" he asked. "How frequent are the cases where force is used, both on duty and off duty, where officers are compelled not to report because they are afraid of getting in trouble?"
In a statement, Toronto police spokesperson Allison Sparkes reiterated that Toronto police contacted the SIU as soon as they learned of their officers' involvement in the death.
"We acknowledge that there are many questions and concerns about this matter," she said.

Late last month, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw issued a statement decrying the fatal beating of Tyre Nichols by five Memphis police officers , saying he condemned the "violent, criminal actions of the officers involved."

Asked if Demkiw would be commenting on the alleged actions of one of his own officers today, Sparkes said, due to the ongoing SIU process and its own internal investigation, the force is "unable to offer further comment at this time so that those proceedings are not compromised."

It is rare for a Toronto police officer to be charged in a homicide. Au is the eighth Toronto officer to face manslaughter or murder charges since the SIU's founding in 1990, according to the Star's archives.

In 2013, the SIU charged former Toronto police officer James Forcillo with second-degree murder after he fatally shot teen Sammy Yatim in Toronto streetcar. The case led to one of the highest-profile murder trials in the city's recent history, and ended with Forcillo convicted of attempted murder - an outcome made possible by Crown prosecutors' rare decision to split the nine shots Forcillo had fired at Yatim in two separate volleys covering separate criminal charges. In 2018, he was sentenced to six years in jail but was granted full parole in 2020.

Toronto police officer David Cavanagh was the first Toronto police officer to face a murder charge. The emergency task force officer was initially charged with manslaughter after what police said was an accidental gun discharge from his MP5 submachine-gun during a September 2010 raid in an Etobicoke residence, a shooting that killed 26-year-old Eric Osawe. The charge was later upgraded to second-degree murder before a judge tossed the case entirely, saying the evidence pointed to an accident .

A handful of other Toronto police officers have been charged with manslaughter in the last few decades; all have been cleared. They include officer Rick Shank, charged and acquitted in the death of Hugh Dawson in 1997, and four other officers - Robert LeMaitre, Phillip Duncan, Nam-Nhat Le and Filippo Bevilacqua - who were charged and cleared of manslaughter in the death of Otto Vass in 2000.

The charges against Au come six months after the SIU charged three Ontario Provincial Police officers with manslaughter after the fatal shootings of a toddler and his father in Kawartha Lakes in late 2020. OPP Constables Nathan Vanderheyden, Kenneth Pengelly and Grayson Cappus each face one count of manslaughter and criminal negligence causing death in relation to the shooting of the boy, 18-month old Jameson Shapiro.
Au is scheduled to make his first court appearance in Brampton on March 2.
